claim: DNA replication requires that the duplex genomic DNA strands be separated by ring-shaped hexameric helicases in all Domains.
source: DNA replication requires that the duplex genomic DNA strands be separated; a function that is implemented by ring-shaped hexameric helicases in all Domains.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about DNA replication mechanisms across all domains of life.

claim: Helicases are composed of two domains: an N-terminal DNA binding domain (NTD) and a C-terminal motor domain (CTD).
source: Helicases are composed of two domains, an N- terminal DNA binding domain (NTD) and a C- terminal motor domain (CTD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about helicase structure.

claim: Both the DNA substrate and the C-terminal winged-helix (WH) domain influence the orientation of Saccharolobus solfataricus MCM on DNA.
source: Our results show that both the DNA substrate and the C-terminal winged-helix (WH) domain influence the orientation but that translocation on DNA proceeds N-first.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from footprinting and unwinding assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Translocation on DNA by Saccharolobus solfataricus MCM proceeds N-first.
source: Our results show that both the DNA substrate and the C-terminal winged-helix (WH) domain influence the orientation but that translocation on DNA proceeds N-first.
evidence: This is the primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches including FRET and unwinding assays.

claim: The hexameric MCM complex is conserved throughout archaea and eukaryotic species as the DNA helicase that unwinds the duplex genome.
source: The hexameric MCM complex is conserved throughout archaea and eukaryotic species as the DNA helicase that unwinds the duplex genome providing leading and lagging strand templates for replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCM conservation across domains.

claim: MCM proteins have a C-terminal domain (CTD) that contains the conserved AAA+ motor domain that provides energy for translocation and DNA unwinding.
source: The MCM proteins themselves are bilobal with a N-terminal domain (NTD) that acts to stabilize binding to single-strand DNA (ssDNA), a C-terminal domain (CTD) that contains the conserved AAA+ (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities) motor domain that provide energy for translocation and DNA unwinding, and a winged-helix (WH) domain for DNA binding (Trakselis, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: DNA unwinding by MCM proceeds by encircling and translocating along the leading strand in the 3'−5' direction, while sterically excluding the lagging strand template.
source: DNA unwinding proceeds by encircling and translocating along the leading strand in the 3'−5' direction, while sterically excluding the lagging strand template (Kelman et al., 1999; Chong et al., 2000; Bochman and Schwacha, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In eukaryotes, six homologous proteins comprise the MCM2-7 heterohexameric complex.
source: In eukaryotes, six homologous proteins comprise the MCM2-7 heterohexameric complex (Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: MCM2-7 interacts with Cdc45 and the GINS heterotetramer to form the active unwinding CMG complex.
source: MCM2-7 interacts with Cdc45 and the GINS heterotetramer (Psf1, 2, 3, Sld5) to form the active unwinding CMG complex (Moyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: GINS binds primarily to the AAA+ CTD of MCM5 bringing in Cdc45 to interact with and close the interface with MCM2.
source: GINS binds primarily to the AAA+ CTD of MCM5 bringing in Cdc45 to interact with and close the interface with MCM2, aligning the motor domains into a proper configuration for activity (Costa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Archaea have a single MCM protein that is equally homologous to the six eukaryotic MCM2-7 proteins.
source: Archaea have a single MCM protein that is equally homologous to the six eukaryotic MCM2-7 proteins (Makarova et al., 2012; Goswami et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Archaeal MCM helicase is active on its own in vitro and does not require accessory proteins for robust DNA unwinding.
source: in contrast to eukaryotes, the archaeal MCM helicase is active on its own in vitro and does not require accessory proteins for robust DNA unwinding (Chong et al., 2000; Marinsek et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Archaeal MCM can interact with orthologs of Cdc45 (RecJ) and the GINS complex to stimulate the helicase activity further.
source: Archaeal MCM forms a homohexameric complex but can also interact with orthologs of Cdc45 (RecJ) and the GINS (GINS23, GINS15) complex to stimulate the helicase activity further (Yoshimochi et al., 2008; Lang and Huang, 2015; Xu et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cdc45 (GAN) is not required for viability in the euryarchaea, Thermococcus kodakarensis.
source: although Cdc45 (i.e. GAN) is not required for viability in the euryarchaea,Thermococcus kodakarensis, possibly implicating this protein as a redundant nuclease for Okazaki fragment maturation (Burkhart et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The consensus origin loaded double hexamer state places the NTDs together with the CTDs facing outwards.
source: but the consensus origin loaded double hexamer state places the NTDs together with the CTDs facing outwards (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The head-to-head orientation achieved during initiation is conserved with the analogous Large-T antigen of SV40 virus.
source: This head-to-head orientation achieved during initiation is also conserved with the analogous Large-T antigen of SV40 virus (Valle et al., 2000; Gomez-Lorenzo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Recent data in the eukaryotic system shows that MCM activation involves cyclin dependent kinases (CDK) firing factors, additional components including MCM10, and ATP hydrolysis by MCM subunits to untwist the dsDNA.
source: Recent data in the eukaryotic system shows this will involve cyclin dependent kinases (CDK) firing factors, additional components including MCM10, and ATP hydrolysis by MCM subunits to untwist the dsDNA to give two independent CMGs that have encircled opposing strands (Douglas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: In yeast, the N-first mechanism of CMG translocation has been confirmed.
source: In yeast, the N-first mechanism of CMG translocation has been confirmed, which involves a physical passing of each helicase to regulate origin firing before establishing the replisome progression complex (RPC) (Georgescu et al., 2017; Douglas et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The binding orientation of the single archaeal MCM hexamer bound on fork DNA has been shown previously to place the CTD near the fork junction, suggesting a C-first mechanism of unwinding.
source: The binding orientation of the single archaeal MCM hexamer bound on fork DNA has been shown previously to place the CTD near the fork junction, suggesting a C-first mechanism of unwinding (McGeoch et al., 2005; Rothenberg et al., 2007; Costa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An X-ray structure of an NTD construct of an archaeal MCM shows ssDNA binding orthogonal to the central channel consistent with either N-first or C-first translocation.
source: An X-ray structure of an NTD construct of an archaeal MCM shows ssDNA binding orthogonal to the central channel consistent with either N-first or C-first translocation (Froelich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: C-first translocation for MCM was analogous to the orientation of the homohexameric Escherichia coli DnaB, which places its CTD RecA motor domain near the duplex region.
source: C-first translocation for MCM was analogous to the orientation of the homohexameric Escherichia coli (E. coli) DnaB, which although it has opposite unwinding polarity (5'−3'), also places its CTD RecA motor domain near the duplex region (Jezewska et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on E. coli DnaB.

claim: The strong homology between the archaeal and eukaryotic DNA replication systems would not suggest significant differences in translocation and unwinding mechanisms of the MCM complexes.
source: The strong homology between the archaeal and eukaryotic DNA replication systems would not suggest significant differences in translocation and unwinding mechanisms of the MCM complexes (Barry and Bell, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on homology and supported by citation.

claim: APB attachment at C682 (C642A mutant) provided the greatest signal shift in mobility when crosslinked to DNA.
source: APB attachment at C682 (C642A mutant) provided the greatest signal shift in mobility when crosslinked to DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant crosslinking and subsequent ssDNA cleavage was detected even in the absence of direct UV light with APB-labeled SsoMCM.
source: APB crosslinking to DNA bases is generally non-specific after activation by UV light (Pendergrast et al., 1992; Nodelman et al., 2017), yet we detected significant crosslinking and subsequent ssDNA cleavage even in the absence of direct UV light (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SsoMCM-APB had many cut sites along the length of both ssDNA substrates favoring positioning at the middle of the ssDNA substrate.
source: Overall, SsoMCM-APB had many cut sites along the length of both ssDNA substrates favoring positioning at the middle of the ssDNA substrate, implicating nonspecific binding orientation at multiple positions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from APB footprinting.

claim: Multiple cleavage sites were detected on the ssDNA region of the labelled strand, suggesting different orientation populations and positioning of SsoMCM.
source: In all situations, multiple cleavage sites were detected on the ssDNA region of the labelled strand (indicated by arrows), suggesting different orientation populations and positioning of SsoMCM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from footprinting experiments.

claim: SsoMCM can bind 3' or 5' ssDNA arms with similar affinities to fork DNA, however when noncomplementary 3' and 5' fork arms are available, there is a preference for binding/encircling the 3'-arm.
source: SsoMCM can bind 3' or 5' ssDNA arms with similar affinities to fork DNA, however when noncomplementary 3' and 5' fork arms are available, there is a preference for binding/encircling the 3'-arm (Rothenberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SsoMCM has a significantly lower binding efficiency (~4 fold less) for duplex DNA over fork substrates measured at the single molecule level.
source: SsoMCM has a significantly lower binding efficiency (~4 fold less) for duplex DNA over fork substrates measured at the single molecule level (Rothenberg et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Anisotropy experiments performed with SsoMCM and duplex DNA show a larger dissociation constant (Kd) over fork substrates.
source: Furthermore, anisotropy experiments performed with SsoMCM and duplex DNA also show a larger dissociation constant (Kd) over fork substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: DNaseI footprinting experiments and Electrophoretic Mobility Shift Assays (EMSA) confirmed complete DNA binding without protection of the duplex region.
source: To test this directly, DNaseI footprinting experiments and Electrophoretic Mobility Shift Assays (EMSA) were performed and confirmed complete DNA binding without protection of the duplex region (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The 5'-excluded strand is protected from ssDNA nuclease digestion upon SsoMCM binding.
source: Previously, we have shown that the 5'-excluded strand is protected from ssDNA nuclease digestion upon SsoMCM binding (Graham et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Titration of large amounts of SsoMCM on fork substrates does not compete off the external excluded strand to favor two hexamers binding.
source: and that titration of large amounts of SsoMCM on fork substrates does not compete off the external excluded strand to favor two hexamers binding (Carney and Trakselis, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The predominate bound species is a stoichiometric single SsoMCM hexamer encircling one ssDNA arm and interacting with the other on the exterior surface.
source: Therefore, the predominate bound species is a stoichiometric single SsoMCM hexamer encircling one ssDNA arm and interacting with the other on the exterior surface, but other minor populations also exist.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: For either cleavage agent (APB or FeBABE), there was a significant ~3:1 preference for placing the CTD closer to the duplex region (C@duplex) on equal arm fork DNA independent of which strand is labelled.
source: For either agent (APB or FeBABE), there was a significant ~3:1 preference for placing the CTD closer to the duplex region (C@duplex) independent of which strand is labelled.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of footprinting data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: APB footprinting studies of the 3'-long arm substrate show that there is nearly a 1.5:1 preference of placing the NTD closer to the duplex region (N@duplex).
source: APB footprinting studies of the 3'-long arm substrate instead show that there is nearly a 1.5:1 preference of placing the NTD closer to the duplex region (N@duplex) (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: There is a significant increase and reversed preference for orientating N@duplex for the 3'-long arm fork substrate over the equal arm fork substrate.
source: There is a significant increase and reversed preference for orientating N@duplex for the 3'-long arm fork substrate over the equal arm fork substrate (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from Figure 1C and Figure 2B.

claim: On the 5'-long arm substrate with a shorter 8 nt 3'-arm, the footprinting orientations were reversed, with a >3:1 preference for C@duplex.
source: Therefore, we repeated APB mapping experiments on an opposite 5'-long arm substrate with a shorter 8 nt 3'-arm (Figure 2C–D). Here, the footprinting orientations were reversed, with a >3:1 preference for C@duplex (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: On long arm fork DNA substrates, SsoMCM can bind either the 3'- or 5'-arm in both orientations, but the preferred 3'-5' polarity is CTD-NTD.
source: Therefore, on these long arm fork DNA substrates, SsoMCM can bind either the 3'- or 5'-arm in both orientations, but the preferred 3'-5' polarity is CTD-NTD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the footprinting data from asymmetric fork substrates.

claim: The WH domain at the C-terminus of SsoMCM is suggested as a substrate recognition or localization domain.
source: The WH domain at the C-terminus of SsoMCM is suggested as a substrate recognition or localization domain (Aravind et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The WH domain in both archaea and eukaryotes is considered important for determining MCM helicase loading and initiation during replication.
source: Moreover, the WH domain in both archaea and eukaryotes is considered important for determining MCM helicase loading and initiation during replication (Samson et al., 2016a; Martinez et al., 2017; Goswami et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The WH domain mediates DNA binding.
source: and mediates DNA binding (Gaudier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SsoMCM-WH mutant shows a loss of orientation specificity on equal arm and 3'-long arm substrates compared with full-length SsoMCM.
source: Footprinting experiments were repeated with APB labelled at either C452 or C456 of SsoMCM–WH on equal arm (Figure 3B) or 3'-long arm (Figure 3D) substrates. The results show a loss of orientation specificity (Figure 3C and E) compared with Figure 1C or 2B.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: SsoMCM WT on equal arm fork substrates specifically loads C@duplex, but when SsoMCM-WH binds the same substrate, it loses a binding preference.
source: As shown above, SsoMCM-WH is likely bound on the equal arm fork DNA in at least four populations (two orientations and on either strand). SsoMCM WT on equal arm fork substrates (Figure 1C) specifically loads C@duplex, but when SsoMCM-WH binds the same substrate, it loses a binding preference (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from Figure 1C and Figure 3C.

claim: When ABP footprinting experiments were repeated with the 3'-long arm substrate, there is a complete loss of orientation specificity on both SsoMCM-WH mutants.
source: When ABP footprinting experiments were repeated with the 3'-long arm substrate, there is a complete loss of orientation specificity on both mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The WH domain of SsoMCM influences the binding orientation of this helicase on equal arm fork DNA to place C@duplex but is less important when engaging ssDNA for translocation.
source: These results show that the WH domain of SsoMCM influences the binding orientation of this helicase on equal arm fork DNA to place C@duplex but that this WH domain is less important for when engaging ssDNA for translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the footprinting data with WH deletion mutants.

claim: The fraction unwound by SsoMCM generally hovers between 0.3 and 0.5 depending on the substrate and conditions.
source: Previously, multiple reports have shown that the fraction unwound by SsoMCM generally hovers between 0.3 and 0.5 depending on the substrate and conditions (Barry et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2011; Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The fork DNA substrate with equal 30 nt arms unwinds 0.26 ± 0.01 fraction of DNA.
source: The fork DNA substrate has four possible SsoMCM binding orientations (N@duplex or C@duplex on either the 5' or 3'-arms) and unwinds 0.26 ± 0.01 fraction of DNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-turnover unwinding assays.

claim: Restricting loading to only the 3'-long arm (8 nt 5'-arm) with only two possible orientations significantly increased the unwound fraction to 0.54 ± 0.03.
source: Instead, restricting loading to only the 3'-long arm (8 nt 5'-arm) with only two possible orientations significantly increased the unwound fraction to 0.54 ± 0.03.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-turnover unwinding assays.

claim: When experiments were repeated with 0 nt at the 5' end, there was 2-fold decrease in unwound product confirming that SsoMCM can translocate over the duplex region of the substrates in the absence of any 5'-arm.
source: When experiments were repeated with 0 nt at the 5' end, there was 2-fold decrease in unwound product confirming that SsoMCM can translocate over the duplex region of the substrates in the absence of any 5'-arm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Background unwinding on the 5'-long arm (with 0 or 8 nt 3'-arm) displays only 0.08 ± 0.01 or 0.13 ± 0.01 fraction unwound, respectively.
source: Background unwinding on the 5'-long arm (with 0 or 8 nt 3'-arm) displays only 0.08 ± 0.01 or 0.13 ± 0.01 fraction unwound, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: An 8 nt 3'-arm is not long enough to facilitate unwinding to any significant degree.
source: Therefore, an 8 nt 3'-arm is not long enough to facilitate unwinding to any significant degree.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low unwinding observed with 8 nt 3'-arm substrates.

claim: The 3'-long arm (with 8 nt 5'-arm) fork substrate enables the most productive fraction of SsoMCM helicases competent for unwinding.
source: Hence, the 3'-long arm (with 8 nt 5'-arm) fork substrate enables the most productive fraction of SsoMCM helicases competent for unwinding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unwinding data from different substrates.

claim: Deletion of the WH motif had no effect on DNA binding affinity but significantly increased DNA unwinding in a steady-state experiment.
source: Previously, deletion of the WH motif had no effect on DNA binding affinity but significantly increased DNA unwinding in a steady-state experiment (Barry et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The –WH mutant showed a significant increase in the unwound product with the fork (0.35 ± 0.01) but a slight decrease with the 3'-long arm (0.46 ± 0.01) compared with WT.
source: The –WH mutant showed a significant increase in the unwound product with the fork (0.35 ± 0.01) (Figure 4B) but a slight decrease with the 3'-long arm (0.46 ± 0.01) (Figure 4C) compared with WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: An increased amount of unwound product with the fork substrate for -WH mutant suggests a loss in specificity for SsoMCM orientation and correlates with the near equal N@duplex and C@duplex cleavage mapping.
source: An increased amount of unwound product with the fork substrate suggests a loss in specificity for SsoMCM orientation and correlates with the near equal N@duplex and C@duplex cleavage mapping (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference connecting unwinding data with footprinting data.

claim: The slight decrease in unwound product with the 3'-long arm for -WH mutant correlates with the fraction of N@duplex mapped for WT (0.57 ± 0.03) or –WH (0.52 ± 0.01) on the same substrate.
source: The slight decrease in unwound product with the 3'-long arm correlates with the fraction of N@duplex mapped for WT (0.57 ± 0.03) (Figure 2B) or –WH (0.52 ± 0.01) (Figure 3E) on the same substrate.
evidence: This is an inference connecting unwinding data with footprinting data.

claim: The flexible WH domain influences the population distribution of binding SsoMCM on fork DNA.
source: Therefore, the flexible WH domain influences the population distribution of binding SsoMCM on fork DNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined footprinting and unwinding data with WH deletion mutants.

claim: The fraction unwound for the equal arm fork substrate, 0.26 ± 0.01, corresponds with a similar footprinting ratio of 0.23 ± 0.03 for N@duplex implicating an N-first translocation orientation.
source: The fraction unwound for the equal arm fork substrate, 0.26 ± 0.01 (Figure 4A), corresponds with a similar footprinting ratio of 0.23 ± 0.03 for N@duplex (Figure 1C) implicating an N-first translocation orientation.
evidence: This is an inference connecting unwinding and footprinting data to determine translocation orientation.

claim: The fraction unwound for the 3'-long arm fork substrate, 0.54 ± 0.03, corresponds with a footprinting ratio of 0.57 ± 0.03 for N@duplex correlating with an N-first translocation mechanism.
source: The fraction unwound for the 3'-long arm fork substrate, 0.54 ± 0.03 (Figure 4A), also corresponds with a footprinting ratio of 0.57 ± 0.03 for N@duplex (Figure 2B) again correlating with an N-first translocation mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference connecting unwinding and footprinting data to determine translocation orientation.

claim: The DNA substrate contains a biotin on the translocating strand (nine bases from the duplex junction) that when bound with streptavidin has been shown to inhibit DNA unwinding.
source: The DNA substrate contains a biotin on the translocating strand (nine bases from the duplex junction) that when bound with streptavidin has been shown to inhibit DNA unwinding (Graham et al., 2011) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The experimental FAM quenching result shows an overall small but significant quenching in fluorescence at 518 nm for both N-terminally and C682 labelled SsoMCMs.
source: The experimental FAM quenching result shows an overall small but significant quenching in fluorescence at 518 nm for both labelled SsoMCMs (Figure 5B) that is consistent with multiple binding populations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The larger quenching for the C-terminally labelled SsoMCM is consistent with a greater distribution that places C@duplex on this semi equal arm fork substrate.
source: Qualitatively, the larger quenching for the C-terminally labelled SsoMCM is consistent with a greater distribution that places C@duplex on this semi equal arm fork substrate (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET data and previous footprinting results.

claim: Binding/loading of SsoMCM labelled at C682 or the N-terminus with Cy3 to fork DNA bound by streptavidin showed similar double exponential increases in Cy3 sensitization with rates of 0.57 ± 0.03 s−1 and 0.030 ± 0.001 s−1 or 0.65 ± 0.02 s−1 and 0.043 ± 0.01 s−1, respectively.
source: Binding/loading of SsoMCM labelled at C682 or the N-terminus with Cy3 to fork DNA bound by streptavidin showed similar double exponential increases in Cy3 sensitization with rates of 0.57 ± 0.03 s−1 and 0.030 ± 0.001 s−1 or 0.65 ± 0.02 s−1 and 0.043 ± 0.01 s−1, respectively. (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exclusion of ATP in the experiment did not significantly change the exponential results, 0.62 ± 0.01 s−1 and 0.043 ± 0.001 s−1, for N-terminally labelled SsoMCM showing that binding is independent of nucleotide.
source: Exclusion of ATP in the experiment did not significantly change the exponential results, 0.62 ± 0.01 s−1 and 0.043 ± 0.001 s−1, for N-terminally labelled SsoMCM showing that binding is independent of nucleotide as shown previously (McGeoch et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: Increases in fluorescence are noted for both N and C-terminal labelled SsoMCM consistent with both orientations bound.
source: Increases in fluorescence are noted for both N and C-terminal labelled SsoMCM consistent with both orientations bound.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET data.

claim: MCM helicases have been shown to displace streptavidin from biotin on the translocating strand, but the rate of this displacement is on the order of hours.
source: Although MCM helicases have been shown to displace streptavidin from biotin on the translocating strand, the rate of this displacement in is on the order of hours.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCM-streptavidin interactions.

claim: No streptavidin displacement was shown in the 5 min experimental time courses for these assays.
source: Our experimental time courses for these assays are 5 min, where no streptavidin displacement was shown previously (Graham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When the Cy3 is labelled at C682, an initial increase (0.53 ± 0.05 s−1) within the first 10 s was noted followed by a slower and more significant decrease in fluorescence (1.1 ± 0.2×10−3 s−1).
source: When the stopped-flow experiment was performed, an initial increase (0.53 ± 0.05 s−1) within the first 10 s was noted followed by a slower and more significant decrease in fluorescence (1.1 ± 0.2×10−3 s−1) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The first faster increase in FRET is consistent with more SsoMCM molecules being bound to the DNA template upon addition of ATP.
source: The first faster increase is consistent with more SsoMCM molecules being bound to the DNA template upon addition of ATP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET data and comparison with loading experiments.

claim: The second slower change in FRET for C682-labeled SsoMCM is consistent with dissociation, but not with C-first translocation.
source: The second slower change is consistent with dissociation, but not with C-first translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET data and expected behavior for C-first translocation.

claim: In the stopped-flow experiment with N-terminal labelled Cy3, there was an initial increase (0.26 ± 0.02 s−1) similar to that seen with the label at C682, followed by a larger and slower increase (1.5 ± 0.4×10−3 s−1) in fluorescence.
source: In the stopped-flow experiment with N-terminal labelled Cy3, there was an initial increase (0.26 ± 0.02 s−1) similar to that seen with the label at C682, followed by a larger and slower increase (1.5 ± 0.4×10−3 s−1) in fluorescence (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The second rate in both FRET experiments (at 57°C) is consistent with the translocation/unwinding rate of SsoMCM at 60°C.
source: The second rate in both experiments (at 57°C) is consistent with the translocation/unwinding rate of SsoMCM at 60°C (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference connecting FRET rates with unwinding rates.

claim: The single turnover unwinding rate for the 3'-long arm substrate is 0.07 ± 0.01 min−1 (or ~ 1.1 ± 0.16 x 10−3 s−1) and is for complete separation of the duplex.
source: The single turnover unwinding rate for the 3'-long arm substrate (Figure 4A) is 0.07 ± 0.01 min−1 (or ~ 1.1 ± 0.16 x 10−3 s−1) and is for complete separation of the duplex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figure 4A.

claim: The second exponential rate in the presteady-state FRET experiments is extremely similar to the single-turnover experiments and only measures translocation up to nine nts or one fourth of the duplex.
source: The second exponential rate in these presteady-state experiments is extremely similar to the single-turnover experiments and only measures translocation up to nine nts or one fourth of the duplex.
evidence: This is an inference comparing FRET and unwinding rates.

claim: When stopped-flow experiments were performed in the absence of streptavidin, similar initial increases are shown for both C682 (0.27 ± 0.01 s−1) and N-terminal (0.21 ± 0.01 s−1) labelled SsoMCM, but slower and similar decreases are shown for both labelled constructs (0.85 ± 0.05×10−3 s−1 and 1.0 ± 0.5×10−3 s−1), respectively.
source: When stopped-flow experiments were performed in the absence of streptavidin, similar initial increases are shown for both C682 (0.27 ± 0.01 s−1) and N-terminal (0.21 ± 0.01 s−1) labelled SsoMCM, but now slower and similar decreases are shown for both labelled constructs (0.85 ± 0.05×10−3 s−1 and 1.0 ± 0.5×10−3 s−1), respectively, consistent with unwinding past the biotin and FAM (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: SsoMCM is known to unwind over small adducts such as biotin on the translocating strand.
source: SsoMCM is known to unwind over small adducts such as biotin on the translocating strand (Graham et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Movement past the FAM label on the excluded strand for both labelled SsoMCMs would result in an increase followed by a larger decrease in FRET upon strand separation that would be stochastically blurred in this time scale.
source: and movement past the FAM label on the excluded strand for both labelled SsoMCMs would result in an increase followed by a larger decrease in FRET upon strand separation that would be stochastically blurred in this time scale.
evidence: This is an inference about expected FRET behavior during unwinding.

claim: SsoMCM can be organized on fork DNA in both orientations with particular probabilities depending on the presence of the excluded strand and the C-terminal WH domain, but translocation and unwinding proceeds N-first in the 3'−5' direction.

evidence: This is an inference based on unwinding and footprinting data.

Using this approach, we could directly monitor the translocation orientation between the NTD of SsoMCM and DNA to verify an N-first translocation mechanism.
